title: How to grade essays faster without losing feedback quality on Mac: a teacher's routine
metaTitle: Grade essays faster without losing feedback quality on Mac
description: Grade essays faster without losing feedback quality. A Mac routine with Pages, Word comments, Dictation and honest notes on AI tools for teachers.
targetKeyword: grade essays faster without losing feedback quality
secondaryKeywords: reduce essay grading time on Mac
intro: To grade essays faster without losing feedback quality, comment on fewer things and comment on them better. Pick a few goals before you open the first essay. Then use Mac tools for the repeated work, so your attention stays on the student's writing. This page covers what grading costs, what the research says, fixes you can start today, and where Lazur helps.
tldr: Comment on a few goals per essay, not on every sentence.
Build a comment bank in Pages or Word, then add one specific line for each student.
Write comments on drafts before you add a grade. Research links grades alone to weaker motivation.
Dictate longer comments with macOS Dictation, then proofread them with Writing Tools.
Lazur points at buttons, dictates at your cursor and drafts starter text. It does not grade for you.

blocks.text: Where grading time actually goes
Grading has two parts: reading the work and writing feedback on it. The mark itself takes seconds. Most of the effort sits in the reading and the commenting, and that is the part you can change.

A 2025 survey of 258 US teachers put average grading time at 9.9 hours a week. Learnosity released that survey, and Learnosity sells assessment software, so treat the number as a rough guide. The same survey found that 95% of teachers take grading work home.

Research points the same way. The Education Endowment Foundation says feedback is not free, and that large amounts of time go into it, perhaps not always productively. Its guidance focuses on the principles of good feedback more than on the method. That gap is your opening. You can keep the principles and drop the wasted steps.

Here is a typical essay. You read it once for meaning. You read it again against the rubric. Then you type three comments you typed on the last essay, and you enter a grade. Each step feels small. Across a full class, the repeats add up.
Which feedback helps student writers most

Graham, Hebert and Harris pooled studies of students in grades 1 to 8. Their weighted effect sizes were 0.87 for adult feedback, 0.62 for self feedback, 0.58 for peer feedback and 0.38 for computer feedback. Adult feedback scored highest. Peer and self feedback were smaller, but they still sat above the computer figure.

Read that chart with care. It measures learning gains across studies. It does not measure how long a teacher spends. The useful question is which comments change a student's next draft, because those are the comments worth your time.
Why grades alone hurt the next draft

Koenka and colleagues (2021) compared grades with comments. Grades improved achievement compared with no feedback, but they also reduced motivation. Students who got grades alone had poorer achievement and less optimal motivation than students who got comments. The analysis pools many studies, not one class.

This does not mean you hide every grade. It means the order matters. On a draft, write comments and leave the grade off. Enter the grade on the final version, when the student has finished revising. That order keeps the comments in focus.
Comment on a few goals, not every sentence

The fastest feedback starts with a short goal list. Pick the few things that matter most for this assignment, such as thesis, evidence and organization. Then work through the batch with those goals in mind, and leave the rest for another round.

items: Write the goals on a note before you start the batch.
Read one essay for each goal, not all goals at once.
Put one comment on the strongest passage and one on the weakest, for each goal.
End with a question the student must answer in the next draft.
Stop when the next comment would repeat one you already wrote.

blocks.text: Notice what is missing. There is no comment on every comma. A student cannot act on a long list of fixes, so the list often goes unused. A short list is kinder to the student and quicker for you.
Build a comment bank you can edit

A comment bank is a document of reusable comments, grouped by goal. Keep it in Pages or Word. Create a new document named Comment bank. Add a heading for each goal, such as Thesis, Evidence and Organization. Under each heading, paste the comments you write most often.

Here is an example for thesis. Your claim in the opening is clear. The second paragraph does not support it yet. Which quote would prove this point? Paste that text, then change one detail so it names the student's own sentence. Generic comments read like form letters, and students skip them.
To add a comment in Pages, select the text, click Comment, then save. The steps are in our guide on [how to add a comment in Pages on Mac](/how-to/add-a-comment-in-pages).
Check your comments with Writing Tools Proofread

Typos in feedback cost you trust. Apple's Writing Tools can proofread a selection on your Mac. Select the text, Control-click it, then choose Writing Tools > Show Writing Tools > Proofread. The feature needs Apple Intelligence, and Apple's page notes region and language limits.

Pages added Writing Tools to proofread text in version 14.3. Pages 15.4 requires macOS 26 or later. Writing Tools work in most apps, including websites, so you can check a comment in a browser too. Read the result before you accept it, because Proofread checks wording, not your judgment about the essay.
Dictate longer comments instead of typing them

Dictation suits long comments, the ones where you explain a reason. Turn it on in System Settings > Keyboard. Then start it with the Dictation shortcut, or choose Edit > Start Dictation in the app. Speak in full sentences, and read the comment back before you save it.

I did not find a controlled study that measures teacher time saved by dictation, rubrics or comment banks. Most time-saving claims come from vendors or from self-reports. Track your own minutes for a few weeks before you decide what to keep.
Use Word comments when students write in Word

Microsoft describes comments as the way to ask questions or suggest corrections without changing the student's text. Track Changes handles edits. Microsoft's help page covers Word for Microsoft 365, Word 2024 and Word 2021 on Mac. Use a comment when the student should decide. Use a tracked change when the fix is mechanical.

blocks.title: Check your Office version
blocks.text: MacRumors reported that Office 2019 for Mac will enter reduced functionality mode from July 13, 2026. In that mode you can open, view and print, but you cannot create, edit or save. Microsoft says reinstalling will not fix it. Check which Office version your school runs.
Where AI helps and where it stops

Most data on AI and grading is self-reported. In a 2025 Gallup-Walton poll, weekly AI users said they save 5.9 hours a week, and monthly users said 2.9 hours. Teachers in schools with an AI policy reported 2.3 hours saved a week, compared with 1.7 hours without one. Those are estimates from teachers, not measured time.

The quality question is still open for this guide. Steiss and colleagues compared human and ChatGPT feedback on student writing in 2024. The results were not available here, so this page does not give a verdict from that paper. Read it before you rely on AI comments for a grade.

Use AI for the sentence-level work you already do yourself, such as a clearer comment or a plainer example of a rubric term. Do not hand it the decision about the grade. Before any student work goes into an AI tool, check your school's rules on student data.
Mistakes that slow you down or lower quality

items: Starting to comment before you read the whole batch once, which makes early and late comments inconsistent.
Writing the same generic comment on every essay.
Giving a grade that does not match the comments beside it.
Dictating a comment and saving it without reading it back.
Letting a bank comment replace a line about the actual essay.
Putting student names or work into an AI tool without checking your school's rules.
Trying to fix everything in one pass.

blocks.text: Edge cases: short drafts, weak writers and multilingual students

Some essays need a different approach. A very weak draft does not need every problem named. Pick the one problem that blocks the rest, such as an unclear claim, and comment on that. A student who gets a short, clear message can act on it.

A reasonable default for multilingual writers is meaning before style. Ask whether the idea reaches the reader. Leave sentence-level fixes for a later draft, or give one example and say it applies everywhere. Check Apple's language limits before you rely on Proofread for a student's language.

Long essays are the hardest case. Read the introduction and conclusion first, then the body. Comment on the passage that carries the argument. Do not annotate the whole essay line by line, because the student will not read every note.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold Option and Command together to ask about anything on your screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a control is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time.

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Lazur can also draft text that you edit before you use it. It does not grade essays, it does not click buttons for you, and it is not an add-in for Pages, Word or Gmail.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Essays contain student work, so check your school's rules before you use Lazur on one.
What to do next

Pick one goal for your next batch. Build a comment bank from the comments you repeat most. Dictate one long comment today and proofread it. Then time one full batch and compare it with your last one. Keep the habits that help, and drop the rest.

faq.question: Will grading faster lower feedback quality?
faq.answer: Not by itself. The EEF guidance says the principles of good feedback matter more than the method. Short, focused comments on a few goals can be sharper than long lists. Speed hurts when you stop checking whether students act on what you wrote.

faq.question: Is there proof that rubrics or comment banks save time?
faq.answer: I did not find a peer-reviewed study that measures teacher time saved by rubrics, comment banks or audio feedback. Most time-saving claims come from vendors or self-reports. Time your own batches for a few weeks before you decide.

faq.question: Can AI grade my essays accurately?
faq.answer: This guide does not give a verdict. A 2024 study compared human and ChatGPT feedback on student writing, but its results were not available here. Use AI for drafts you edit, and keep the grade decision with you.

faq.question: Can I paste student essays into Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur sees your screen only while you hold the shortcut. The screenshot and audio go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Check your school's rules on student data first, because some schools limit AI tools for student work.

faq.question: Do I need Microsoft 365 to grade in Word?
faq.answer: Yes, if you want Word. Microsoft lists Word in Microsoft 365 Personal, which costs $99.99 a year at the US list price. You do not need Microsoft 365 to use Pages comments or macOS Dictation.

faq.question: Does Proofread work on comments written in a browser?
faq.answer: Apple says Writing Tools work in most apps, including third-party apps and websites. Select the text in your browser, then Control-click it. Read the result before you accept it, because Proofread checks wording only.

faq.question: What if my school uses Google Docs?
faq.answer: The same routine works. This guide did not research Google Docs comment features or menu paths, so check Google's own help before you rely on them. Our [Google Docs guide for teachers](/for/teachers/google-docs) covers more.

faq.question: How do I know whether the changes are working?
faq.answer: Measure, do not guess. Time one batch before you change anything, then time a batch after your changes. Self-reported savings vary widely, so your own timing is the number that counts.

costs.title: Your evenings and weekends
costs.text: Learnosity's 2025 survey of 258 US teachers found an average of 9.9 hours a week on grading. It also found 95% of teachers take grading work home. The survey was run by a vendor and used a small sample, so read it as a signal, not a census.

costs.title: Your health and your job
costs.text: RAND's 2025 survey, reported by EdWeek, found more than 80% of teachers work beyond contracted hours, about 10 extra hours a week. Only half said they were satisfied with their workload. Burnout fell to 53% from 60% in 2024. Learnosity also reported that 32% of teachers cite grading demands as a reason to consider leaving.

costs.title: Feedback that eats time without helping
costs.text: The EEF guidance says feedback is not free. It also says large amounts of time go to feedback, perhaps not always productively. If students do not act on your comments, the time buys very little for them or for you.

costs.title: Students who get grades alone
costs.text: Koenka and colleagues found that grades reduced motivation compared with comments. Students who got grades alone had poorer achievement than students who got comments. A grade-only return spends your hours and gives the student less back.

causes.title: You write the same comments again
causes.text: Many essays in one class share the same problems. Writing those comments from scratch on each essay wastes time. Comments also drift as you tire, so early and late essays can get different feedback.

causes.title: You read every essay twice
causes.text: You read once to understand and again to check the rubric and find evidence for each comment. Two passes feel thorough. They also double the reading. A short goal list lets you read once with a clear target.

causes.title: The feedback has no focus
causes.text: EEF guidance says the principles of good feedback matter more than the method. Without a focus, feedback turns into a list of every error. Students cannot act on that much at once, and you cannot finish writing it.

causes.title: Grades are entered too early
causes.text: When you grade a draft, you start defending a number. The comments then justify the grade instead of helping the next draft. Koenka and colleagues found grades alone weaker for motivation than comments.

causes.title: Your tools break your flow
causes.text: Switching between the grading portal, Pages, Gmail and a timer costs attention each time. Each switch is small. Across a whole batch, the switches add up to real lost time.

causes.title: Typing is the slowest step
causes.text: A long, explained comment takes the most typing. Speaking the same reason can be faster, but you must read it back. Short bank comments with one specific edit are faster still.

causes.title: Every line gets a comment
causes.text: When every line gets a note, the most important problem looks like one more problem. Students see a page of marks and miss the one change that would matter most.

fixes.title: Set a goal list before the batch
fixes.text: Write a short goal list, such as thesis, evidence and organization, before you open the first essay. Keep it in view. Comment only on those goals this round. Note other issues for a later round, not on this essay.

fixes.title: Read the batch once per goal
fixes.text: Read the whole batch for the first goal, then again for the next. Start with the goal that blocks the rest, such as an unclear claim. Holding one standard at a time makes your comments easier to keep consistent.

fixes.title: Build a comment bank in Pages or Word
fixes.text: Create one document named Comment bank. Group comments under goal headings. Copy a bank comment into place, then add one line about the actual essay. Edit before you send.

fixes.title: Proofread comments with Writing Tools
fixes.text: Select your comment, Control-click it, then choose Writing Tools > Show Writing Tools > Proofread. It needs Apple Intelligence. Read the result before you accept it, because it checks wording, not your judgment.

fixes.title: Dictate long comments, then read them back
fixes.text: Turn on Dictation in System Settings > Keyboard. Use Edit > Start Dictation for the comments that explain a reason. Read each one back before you save it, and fix names and facts by hand.

fixes.title: Write drafts without a grade
fixes.text: On drafts, write comments and leave the grade off. The research on grades and comments points toward comments for motivation. Enter the grade on the final version, when revising is done.

fixes.title: Time your batches before and after
fixes.text: Note how long each batch takes for a few weeks. Compare the weeks. Keep only the changes that cut time without making your comments thinner.

plan.label: Before
plan.title: Choose your goals
plan.text: Write a short goal list for this assignment, such as thesis, evidence and organization. Keep it on paper or in one note. Keep it in view for the whole batch.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Read the batch for one goal
plan.text: Read every essay for the first goal only. Leave one comment per essay. Use your comment bank for common problems, and add one specific line for each student.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Read for the next goal
plan.text: Repeat the pass with the next goal. Proofread your comments with Writing Tools before you return anything. Stop when the next comment would repeat an earlier one.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Dictate the long comments
plan.text: Use macOS Dictation for comments that explain a reason. Read each one back before you save. Type the short edits and student names yourself.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Return and track
plan.text: Return feedback with one question the student must answer in the next draft. Note how long the batch took, so you can compare it with last week.

plan.label: Weekly
plan.title: Update the comment bank
plan.text: Move any comment you used more than once into the bank. Delete comments you rarely use. Keep the bank short enough to scan in seconds.
